The Ochraceous bulbul (Alophoixus ochraceus) is a medium-sized passerine inhabiting evergreen and montane forests across Southeast Asia. Eggs of this species, measuring approximately 25 millimeters in length and 17.5 millimeters in width, produce hatchlings with an initial wet weight of 4 grams [Ww0 = 4 grams]. This modest neonatal mass is typical for bulbuls and reflects the energetic constraints of yolk provisioning. Under incubation temperatures of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the incubation period lasts approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days], a duration consistent with other members of the Pycnonotidae. The relatively short embryonic development period is likely an adaptation to reduce nest predation risk in tropical environments where predator density is high. Field observations indicate that the eggs are entirely dependent on maternal and occasional paternal incubation, with the female assuming the primary role during the night.

Once hatched, the nestling chick enters a phase of rapid growth characterized by feather development and mass gain. Under the typical thermal conditions experienced by actively growing chicks, which maintain body temperatures near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the age at fledging is approximately 16 days after hatching [tx = approximately 16 days after hatching]. This relatively brief nestling period positions the species among the faster-developing bulbuls, an attribute that may facilitate multiple breeding attempts within a single season. During this period, the altricial nestlings are fed primarily by the female, with the male contributing to provisioning duties as the chicks near fledging. The pin-feathered chicks increase their body mass substantially, transitioning from the initial 4 grams to a pre-fledging mass of roughly 20 grams, though this value varies considerably with local food availability and brood size.

Sexual maturation in the Ochraceous bulbul follows a predictable developmental trajectory when birds maintain a body temperature near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty is reached at 48 days after hatching [tp = 48 days after hatching], a remarkably early age for a passerine of this body size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid attainment of reproductive competence suggests that juvenile birds may be physiologically capable of breeding within their first season, although ecological constraints such as territory acquisition and social dominance often delay actual reproductive attempts. The accelerated development of the gonadal axis is supported by a high basal metabolic rate; respirometry trials have confirmed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 68.44 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 68.44 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], reflecting the elevated energetic demands of a fast life-history strategy.

Despite the early onset of puberty, the first successful breeding event is typically deferred. Under conditions of sustained body temperatures around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the age at first brood averages 511 days after hatching [tR = 511 days after hatching], a delay that contrasts sharply with the early pubertal development. This temporal gap likely reflects the need to acquire a high-quality territory and establish a stable pair bond before investing in reproduction. Reproductive output per clutch is modest, with females typically laying 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch] and producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. The combination of a small clutch and limited annual breeding frequency yields a low maximum reproductive rate, suggesting that population growth is constrained by this conservative investment strategy.

Adult female Ochraceous bulbuls attain a maximum body mass of 41.45 grams [Wwi = 41.45 grams], a value consistent with females of other medium-bodied bulbuls in the genus Alophoixus. When maintained at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], wild-caught individuals have been documented to live for approximately 7.1 years [am = approximately 7.1 years], a longevity that is relatively high for a passerine of this mass and reproductive rate. The species is therefore characterized by a life-history syndrome that includes rapid early development, delayed first reproduction, a low annual reproductive output, and an extended adult lifespan—a combination that positions the Ochraceous bulbul as a relatively slow-breeding, long-lived tropical songbird within its ecological community.
